summary.text:
The internal borrowing has almost run out. A year ago Worcestershire funded £123.9m of its capital spending from its own cash. At 31 March 2026 that is £27.7m. The budget assumed £95.8m would still be there. The gap was closed by going to the market: external borrowing rose £118.1m in a single year, from £607.1m to £725.2m, and cash and equivalents halved from £31.5m to £15.7m.

The report says why, and it is not the capital programme. The council carries a £180.8m High Needs deficit on the Dedicated Schools Grant, and its own balance-sheet analysis says that deficit 'is impacting the resource-base of the balance sheet'. Officers have borrowed short deliberately, expecting a High Needs Stability Grant of around £162m before the end of 2026/27. That is a coherent bridge. It is also a bet on a grant arriving.

It has cost two disclosed breaches of the council's own prudential limits. 31.1% of debt now matures within a year — £225.2m against an upper limit of 25% — and the report states plainly that the short-borrowing decision caused it. Separately, other long-term liabilities of £129.4m sit above both the £126.5m operational boundary and the authorised limit, which the report explains as a paper reassessment under IFRS 16 rather than new debt. Both are declared rather than buried, which is the right way round.

The borrowing itself is sensibly built. £508.9m of PWLB at 3.8% over 13.6 years and £80.6m of energy-from-waste borrowing at 3.1% over 16 years are cheap, long money. Against that sit £104.2m borrowed from other councils at 4.3% with 0.7 years to run — the bridging money — and £31.5m of LOBOs at 4.5%. Treasury came in £6.4m better than budget, with interest payable £2.1m under and investment income £1.5m over.

The capital financing requirement closed at £882.3m against a £810.7m budget — £71.6m above, in a report that does not remark on it. And the council's own risk assessment for this report is current risk: HIGH.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your 2025/26 treasury outturn. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

Scope first, because our file is only part of your book. We hold 80 PWLB loans for Worcestershire at a balance of £499.8m against the £589.5m of PWLB you report at 31 March — four months apart — and your £104.2m borrowed from other councils sits outside a PWLB file entirely. We can schedule 72 of the 80; the other eight are excluded from anything below.

The number that made us write is the internal borrowing. A year ago you funded £123.9m of capital spending from your own cash. At 31 March it is £27.7m, and the budget had assumed £95.8m would still be there. External borrowing rose £118.1m in a single year and cash and equivalents halved from £31.5m to £15.7m.

Your report is clear that this is not the capital programme — it is the £180.8m High Needs deficit, with your own balance sheet analysis saying that deficit "is impacting the resource-base of the balance sheet". Borrowing short deliberately, expecting a High Needs Stability Grant of around £162m before the end of 2026/27, is a coherent bridge and we have no view on whether it is the right one. It is your call and you have set out the reasoning openly, including the two disclosed breaches it cost — 31.1% of debt maturing within a year, £225.2m against a 0–25% limit.

What we would offer is the thing the bridge is exposed to. £225.2m rolling inside twelve months means the cost of the bridge is set by the short end on the days you happen to be in the market, not by anything decided in advance. One-year certainty closed at 4.95% this afternoon on notice 314/26 and two-year at 5.06%, against your £104.2m of local authority money currently at 4.3% with an average maturity of 0.7 years. The market-implied path from SONIA has the one-year at 4.11% and two-year at 4.21% — that is what is priced rather than what anyone forecasts, and it is the object that tells you whether waiting is cheap or expensive. We publish it daily and we do not publish forecasts, deliberately.

The other half is depth rather than price. July's sector borrowing was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%. When a bridge depends on being able to roll a quarter of a billion on schedule, how many lenders are actually active that month is not a detail. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

One thing from our own data, offered as information rather than suggestion. 58 of the 72 loans we can price sit below par on the DMO's premature repayment curve today, for about £78.3m of net discount, against 14 above. Standard caveats and we mean them: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, only the DMO can quote, and with a live liquidity bridge running it is plainly not the moment for anything clever. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis if it is ever useful.

Two smaller notes. Your CFR came in at £882.3m against an £810.7m budget — £71.6m above, which the report does not comment on and which we mention only because it moves everything downstream of it. And MRP came in at £14.0m against £16.8m budgeted.

On training, four fit Worcestershire. Liquidity & cashflow forecasting and SONIA Forward Curve & OIS are the two that speak directly to a short-dated bridge. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice, given internal borrowing has gone from £123.9m to £27.7m in a year. And PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
